E00: We wrote the code and tested it with a fake scripted model. It works, but a fake model tells us nothing about the real one.
E01: We set up the cloud machine and probed the real model. It is reachable, supports tool calls and a seed, and gave the same answer to a short prompt.
E02: We found the rate limit (100 requests per minute per key) and that each call reports its own cost. The key budget is $50.
E03: First real test on the two dev tasks, with a step cap of 8. Clean runs pass and the wrong claim spreads, but some agents run out of steps.
E04: Our reading of E03: A5 hit the step cap in 9 unplanned runs. The wrong claim (FA1) always spread. The model ignored the malicious text.
E05: We raised the step cap from 8 to 12.
E06: First repeat check: the grades looked almost the same across repeats. This was corrected later in E10.
E07: We wrote down what we expected from the second test before running it.
E08: Second real test with step cap 12. The problem is fixed: only the runs with a designed timeout are degraded.
E09: Our reading of E08: the step cap was the cause. The stale post did not fool the model. Restart-and-keep-the-board recovered, maybe by lucky ranking.
E10: Correction: the board text differs in every group of repeats, so repeats are real samples. We keep 3 repeats.
E11: Status check of the Phase 1C gate. All criteria are met. The prompts are frozen.
E12: Timing check: one process uses about 75 of the 100 allowed calls per minute, so we run one job at a time.
E13: First test of the always-verify baseline (M3). The verifier's answers can be read. Four runs were skipped by mistake.
E14: We set concurrency to 1 and made the runner report unfinished runs instead of skipping them.
E15: Review of M3: the fault was injected after the verifier, and two of four rejections were false alarms.
E16: We added a clean-run table, a cost column, and the verifier prompt hash in every run record.
E17: The unfinished runs came from a Ctrl-C. We also wrote the sync routine into the AWS runbook.
E18: Decisions: inject the wrong claim before the verifier, and rewrite the verifier prompt to be more precise. Predictions were written before the rerun.
E19: M3 rerun: no false alarms, but no catches either. M3 costs about a third more and changes no grades. It also corrects a count in E18.
E20: The faulty posts contradicted themselves, yet the verifier accepted them. It checked form, not content. We keep M3 as it is for Phase 1.
E21: Plain summary of M3: what it is, how our beliefs changed, where the weakness sits. Idea held for Phase 2: use a different model as the verifier.
E22: Shake-out on the six eval tasks: 30 of 30 runs finished and 29 passed. Runs got slower, so the matrix may take about 4 hours.
E23: We moved to the new instance mccr-2 (Python 3.12 through uv, 171 tests passed) and wrote down what we expected from the matrix.
E24: The matrix: 522 new runs, 0 failed. The wrong claim spread every time, the model refused every attack, and restart-and-keep-the-board recovered every run, against our hypothesis.
E25: Why M1 recovered: A1 runs again and writes a correct post, and A3 follows the newer post. The bad posts stay on the board.
E26: We added two metrics that pass does not see: wrong orders already sent (7) and tainted posts left live (M1 leaves them, M2 does not).
E27: A report table of every metric per mode. Every 'forbidden attempt' was an agent listing the root folder, which is blocked, so it is shown apart.
E28: Three stress cells test the reasons from E25: a persistent fault (FA4), a consistent claim (FA5) and a late wrong revision (FA6). Also a duplicate-order metric. Expectations written before the run.
E29: Stress results: with a persistent fault (FA4), restart-and-keep-the-board recovered 0 of 18 and sent wrong orders twice, while wipe-all recovered all. A post labelled as a revision can beat a newer correct post.
E30: We added wasted and retained work, the report figures, and the trace checks as a script. About a quarter of a full restart's calls redo valid work, which is the most selective recovery could save here.
